questions.title: Genetic information essential for bacterial life
questions.question: Genetic information essential for the life of bacteria is a function of?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein; they carry no genetic (DNA) information of their own and are not the source of the cell's essential genetic instructions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plasmid carries accessory genetic information (such as antibiotic resistance or virulence genes) that is helpful but not essential -- a bacterium can survive without any plasmid at all, unlike its chromosome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane, a structural feature rather than a repository of genetic information.
explanations.D: Correct. The bacterial chromosome carries the genetic information essential for the cell's life -- the core genes required for basic survival and reproduction -- and every living bacterial cell must have one, unlike accessory elements such as plasmids, which a cell can live without. This essential-versus-accessory distinction is exactly what separates the chromosome from a plasmid: both carry genetic information, but only the chromosome's is indispensable.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bacterial chromosome, not the plasmid, ribosomes or mesosomes, carries the genetic information essential for bacterial life.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.author_notes: Near-literal repeat of this same fact recurs at Ch4 Q52 (same four terms, reordered options), held as a duplicate of this question rather than authored twice.

questions.title: Essential structures in a bacterial cell
questions.question: The following are essential structure in bacterial cell?

explanations.A: Correct. The nuclear body (the nucleoid) is the cytoplasmic region holding the bacterial chromosome, and it is an essential structure. Every living bacterial cell must have this single circular chromosome carrying its core genetic information. None of the other structures listed here is required the same way -- every bacterium needs its chromosome to survive, but not every bacterium needs fimbriae, inclusion granules, a plasmid, or a capsule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fimbriae assist adherence in some bacteria but are not present in, or required by, every bacterial cell; they are an accessory rather than essential structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inclusion granules are optional intracellular nutrient-storage deposits (such as glycogen or polyphosphate); a bacterium can live without accumulating them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A plasmid carries accessory (not essential) genetic information; many bacteria live entirely without any plasmid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A capsule is an accessory virulence structure found in some, not all, bacterial species; it is not required for basic bacterial survival.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the nuclear body (nucleoid/chromosome) as an essential bacterial structure, distinguishing it from accessory structures (fimbriae, inclusion granules, plasmid, capsule).

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: A non-essential bacterial structure
questions.question: The following structure is not essential in bacterial cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this structure is essential, so it is not the answer). Ribosomes are required in every bacterial cell to translate mRNA into the proteins the cell needs to survive.
explanations.B: Incorrect (essential). The plasma membrane is required in every bacterial cell as the selectively permeable barrier controlling what enters and leaves the cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect (essential, by standard teaching). The cell wall gives the bacterial cell its shape and rigidity and protects it from osmotic lysis; it is treated as an essential structure in standard bacterial-cell teaching (Mycoplasma, which naturally lacks one, is the recognised exception rather than the rule).
explanations.D: Correct. Fimbriae are accessory surface appendages that assist adherence to surfaces or host cells in some bacteria, but they are not required for a bacterial cell's basic survival -- many bacteria live and divide perfectly well without any fimbriae. This makes fimbriae the one structure in this list that is not essential, unlike ribosomes, the cell membrane, and the cell wall, all of which every standard bacterial cell needs.

questions.learning_objective: Identify fimbriae as a non-essential bacterial structure, distinguishing it from the essential ribosomes, cell membrane and cell wall.

questions.title: Gene: a DNA segment with specific information
questions.question: Segment of DNA that carries in its sequence specific information?

explanations.A: Correct. A gene is, by definition, a segment of DNA whose nucleotide sequence carries specific information -- typically the instructions for one protein or RNA product. This segment-level scale is exactly what distinguishes "gene" from the broader terms genome (a cell's entire DNA) and genotype (the cell's full set of genetic determinants), both of which describe collections of genes rather than one segment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The genome is the entire collection of DNA within a cell, not one segment carrying one piece of specific information.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The genotype is the set of genetic determinants an organism carries, a description of its whole genetic makeup, not a single DNA segment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The phenotype is an organism's observable, expressed characteristics -- not a DNA segment at all, but the outward result of gene expression.

questions.learning_objective: Define a gene as a DNA segment carrying specific information, distinguishing it from genome, genotype and phenotype.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Genotype: the set of genetic determinants
questions.question: A Set of genetic determinants within the cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A gene is one DNA segment carrying specific information, not the entire set of genetic determinants a cell carries.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The genome is the entire collection of DNA (every gene and non-coding sequence together); "genotype" specifically names the set of genetic determinants (genes/alleles), a related but distinct framing of the cell's genetic makeup.
explanations.C: Correct. The genotype is, by definition, the set of genetic determinants an organism carries within its cells -- its underlying genetic makeup. This is distinguished from the phenotype, which is the organism's observable, expressed characteristics (the outward result of that genotype interacting with gene regulation and environment), not the underlying genetic determinants themselves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The phenotype is the organism's observable, expressed characteristics, the product of the genotype being expressed -- not the set of genetic determinants itself.

questions.learning_objective: Define genotype as the set of genetic determinants within the cell, distinguishing it from gene, genome and phenotype.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Genome: the entire collection of a cell's DNA
questions.question: The entire collection of DNA within a cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A gene is one segment of DNA carrying specific information, not the entire collection of a cell's DNA.
explanations.B: Correct. The genome is, by definition, the entire collection of DNA present within a cell -- every gene and every non-coding sequence together. This total-DNA scale is exactly what distinguishes "genome" from "gene" (one segment) and from "genotype" (the set of genetic determinants, a framing focused on the organism's specific alleles rather than on the physical DNA molecule as a whole).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The genotype is the set of genetic determinants an organism carries -- a description of its genetic makeup -- rather than a term for the entire physical DNA collection itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The phenotype is the organism's observable, expressed characteristics, not a description of its DNA content at all.

questions.learning_objective: Define genome as the entire collection of DNA within a cell, distinguishing it from gene, genotype and phenotype.

questions.title: Number of chromosomes in bacteria
questions.question: Bacteria have?

explanations.A: Correct. Bacteria are haploid organisms that typically carry their essential genetic information on a single circular chromosome, held free in the cytoplasm within the nucleoid rather than inside a membrane-bound nucleus. This single-chromosome arrangement is one of the defining features of a prokaryotic cell, in contrast to eukaryotic cells, which can carry multiple chromosomes within a true nucleus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multiple chromosomes is not the standard bacterial arrangement -- bacteria are typically haploid with one circular chromosome, not two.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Three chromosomes is not the standard bacterial arrangement; bacteria are typically haploid with a single chromosome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Four chromosomes is not the standard bacterial arrangement; bacteria are typically haploid with a single chromosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacteria typically have a single circular chromosome (are haploid), not multiple chromosomes.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Plasmid: extrachromosomal DNA replicating independently
questions.question: Extrachromosomal DNA that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A transposon is a mobile DNA sequence that moves between sites in the genome; unlike a plasmid, it does not replicate autonomously as an independent extrachromosomal unit.
explanations.B: Correct. A plasmid is, by definition, a small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA molecule that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome, typically carrying accessory genes (such as antibiotic-resistance or virulence genes) rather than the cell's essential genetic information. This independent-replication property is exactly what distinguishes a plasmid from the bacterial chromosome itself (which it does not depend on to replicate) and from a transposon (which cannot replicate on its own at all).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The chromosome is the cell's own essential genetic material, not an extrachromosomal element -- it is the very structure "extrachromosomal" is defined in contrast to.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A gene is a segment of DNA carrying specific information, not itself an independently replicating extrachromosomal structure.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a plasmid as extrachromosomal DNA that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome, distinct from a transposon, the chromosome, or a gene.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Episome: a chromosome-integrating plasmid
questions.question: Plasmids able to integrate into the host chromosome?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A mesosome is an infolding of the bacterial plasma membrane, not a plasmid, and has no capacity to integrate into the chromosome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A polysome is a cluster of ribosomes simultaneously translating one mRNA; it is not a genetic element and cannot integrate into the chromosome.
explanations.C: Correct. An episome is, by definition, a plasmid that is additionally able to integrate into the bacterial host chromosome (and subsequently replicate along with it), while retaining the ability to also exist and replicate independently in the cytoplasm like an ordinary plasmid. This dual capability -- independent replication or chromosome integration -- is exactly what the term "episome" is used to single out.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribosomes are the cell's protein-synthesis machinery, made of rRNA and protein; they are not genetic elements and cannot integrate into the chromosome.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an episome as a plasmid able to integrate into the host chromosome, distinguishing it from mesosomes, polysomes and ribosomes.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Pathogenicity islands: mobile virulence-gene elements
questions.question: Special class of mobile genetic elements containing virulence genes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An episome is a plasmid additionally able to integrate into the host chromosome; it is defined by that integrating capability, not specifically by carrying virulence genes.
explanations.B: Correct. Pathogenicity islands (PAIs) are, by definition, the special class of mobile genetic element specifically characterised by carrying a cluster of virulence genes. Acquiring a PAI can convert a relatively harmless bacterial strain into a more pathogenic one, which is exactly the virulence-gene-carrying property this question is testing, and is what sets PAIs apart from the other, more general-purpose mobile elements listed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A plasmid is a broad category of extrachromosomal DNA that may or may not carry virulence genes; it is not the class specifically defined by that property the way a pathogenicity island is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An insertion sequence is a simple mobile genetic element that typically carries only the genes needed for its own transposition, not a cluster of virulence genes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pathogenicity islands (PAIs) as the mobile genetic element class specifically defined by carrying virulence genes, distinct from episomes, plasmids and insertion sequences.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Adenine-thymine base pairing bonds
questions.question: Adenine pairs with thymine through?

explanations.A: Correct. Adenine pairs with thymine through 2 hydrogen bonds in double-stranded DNA -- fewer than the 3 hydrogen bonds that hold a guanine-cytosine pair together. This difference in bond count is why AT-rich DNA regions are comparatively easier to separate (denature/melt) than GC-rich regions, which have proportionally more hydrogen bonds resisting strand separation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 3 hydrogen bonds is the number holding a guanine-cytosine pair together, not an adenine-thymine pair.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neither base pair in DNA is held by 4 hydrogen bonds; the two possible counts are 2 (A-T) and 3 (G-C).
explanations.D: Incorrect. 6 hydrogen bonds does not describe either standard DNA base pair; the two possible counts are 2 (A-T) and 3 (G-C).

questions.learning_objective: State that adenine pairs with thymine through 2 hydrogen bonds, fewer than guanine-cytosine's 3.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Leading strand: continuous DNA synthesis
questions.question: Newly formed strand of DNA synthesized continuously?

explanations.A: Correct. The leading strand is, by definition, synthesized continuously, as one unbroken piece, in the same direction as the replication fork's movement, because DNA polymerase can extend it 5' to 3' without interruption as the fork opens up new template ahead of it. This continuous synthesis is the direct opposite of the lagging strand's fragmented, discontinuous synthesis on the other template strand of the same replication fork.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lagging strand is synthesized intermittently (discontinuously), as short fragments later joined together -- the opposite of continuous synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A primer is a short RNA (or DNA) segment that provides a starting 3'-OH for DNA polymerase; it is not itself a name for continuously synthesized DNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Complementary strand" is a generic term for either newly made strand (leading or lagging); it does not specifically name the continuously synthesized one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the leading strand as the DNA strand synthesized continuously, distinct from the lagging strand, primer, or complementary strand generically.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Lagging strand: intermittent DNA synthesis
questions.question: Newly formed strand of DNA synthesized intermittently?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The leading strand is synthesized continuously, as one unbroken piece -- the opposite of intermittent synthesis.
explanations.B: Correct. The lagging strand is, by definition, synthesized intermittently (discontinuously), because it runs in the direction opposite to the replication fork's movement and DNA polymerase can only extend DNA 5' to 3'. It is therefore built as a series of short fragments (Okazaki fragments), each needing its own new primer, which are only later joined together by DNA ligase -- the direct opposite of the leading strand's single continuous synthesis on the other template.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A primer is a short segment that starts each new fragment on the lagging strand; it is not itself the name for the intermittently synthesized strand as a whole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Complementary strand" is a generic term for either newly made strand (leading or lagging); it does not specifically name the intermittently synthesized one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the lagging strand as the DNA strand synthesized intermittently (discontinuously), distinct from the leading strand, primer, or complementary strand generically.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: First event after temperate phage infection
questions.question: When a temperate bacteriophage infects a bacterial cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The phage's DNA does not immediately replicate itself on entering the cell -- the first molecular event is transcription of its own early genes.
explanations.B: Correct. Immediately after a temperate bacteriophage's DNA enters a bacterial cell, the first molecular event is transcription of the phage's own early genes, using the host cell's RNA polymerase -- not replication, translation, or conjugation. It is the products of this early transcription that ultimately determine, through the regulatory proteins made, whether the cell commits to the lytic pathway or establishes lysogeny by integrating the phage genome as a prophage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Translation (making protein from mRNA) can only happen after the phage's early genes have first been transcribed into mRNA -- transcription necessarily comes before translation, not the other way around, as the first event.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conjugation is an entirely separate gene-transfer mechanism between two bacterial cells via a sex pilus; it plays no part in what happens inside a single cell immediately after a phage infects it.

questions.learning_objective: State that transcription of early phage genes is the immediate event following temperate-phage infection, before replication, translation or the lysis-vs-lysogeny commitment.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.author_notes: Same stem as Ch3 Q1 ("When a temperate bacteriophage infects a bacterial cell?") but a wholly different option set (Replication/Transcription/Translation/Conjugation vs Ch3 Q1's phage-behaviour options) testing a finer-grained, sequential fact -- authored as a distinct question, not held as a duplicate.

questions.title: Why bacteria regulate gene expression
questions.question: Bacteria have Regulatory system for gene expression to?

options.A: To be adapted to any environmental changes
options.C: To avoid production of all catabolic and anabolic enzymes continuously

explanations.A: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Adapting to environmental change is one genuine purpose of gene regulation, but only one of three listed here, not the complete answer by itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Conserving the cell's limited resources by not making unneeded proteins is a genuine purpose, but again only one of three.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone (true but partial). Avoiding the wasteful continuous production of every catabolic and anabolic enzyme is a genuine purpose, but still only one of three.
explanations.D: Correct. Bacterial gene regulation serves all three purposes jointly: it lets the cell adapt to changing environmental conditions, it conserves the cell's limited resources by not synthesizing unneeded proteins, and it specifically avoids the wasteful continuous production of every catabolic and anabolic enzyme regardless of whether its substrate is present. Since every one of the three listed statements is independently true and none contradicts the others, "all of the above" is the composite correct answer rather than any single purpose alone.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that bacterial gene regulation jointly serves environmental adaptation, resource conservation, and avoiding constitutive enzyme production.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Mutation: a permanent change in DNA sequence
questions.question: A permanent change in DNA sequence?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Replication is the copying of DNA to make an identical new molecule; when accurate, it does not itself alter the sequence -- it is not what "mutation" names.
explanations.B: Correct. A mutation is, by definition, a permanent change in an organism's DNA sequence -- and because that change is copied into every subsequent generation of the cell, it is also a heritable alteration of the genome. This distinguishes mutation sharply from replication, transcription and conjugation, none of which are themselves alterations of the underlying genetic sequence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transcription is the process of making RNA from a DNA template; it reads the existing sequence without permanently changing it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conjugation is a mechanism of transferring DNA between two bacterial cells; it is a transfer process, not itself a permanent alteration of a DNA sequence.

questions.learning_objective: Define mutation as a permanent change in DNA sequence, distinguishing it from replication, transcription and conjugation.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.author_notes: A near-literal repeat of this same fact recurs at Ch4 Q54 ("Heritable changes in genome are called?"), authored as its own distinct question rather than held, since it reuses the same concept from a genuinely different qualifying angle (heritability of the genome vs permanence of the sequence).

questions.title: Mutagenic factors: the exception
questions.question: All of the following are mutagenic factors EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a genuine mutagen, so not the EXCEPT answer). Ionising radioactivity directly damages DNA and is a classic, recognised mutagenic factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect (genuine mutagen). UV rays damage DNA (classically by forming pyrimidine dimers) and are a standard recognised mutagen.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Disinfectants are antimicrobial agents whose primary action is killing or inhibiting microorganisms -- typically by disrupting cell membranes or denaturing proteins -- rather than acting as DNA-damaging mutagens, so they are not grouped with the recognised mutagenic factors the way radioactivity, UV rays and alkylating chemicals are.
explanations.D: Incorrect (genuine mutagen). Alkylating chemicals directly modify DNA bases and are a standard recognised class of chemical mutagen.

questions.learning_objective: Identify radioactivity, UV rays and alkylating chemicals as mutagenic factors, and disinfectants as the exception.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Parasexuality: unilateral gene transfer
questions.question: Unilateral transfer of genetic information from a donor cell to a recipient cell are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Binary fission is ordinary asexual bacterial division of one cell into two identical daughters; it involves no transfer of genetic material between two separate cells at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transformation is one specific mechanism by which unilateral gene transfer can occur (uptake of free DNA), not the general term for the unilateral donor-to-recipient pattern itself.
explanations.C: Correct. "Parasexuality" is the general term for bacteria's unilateral, one-way pattern of genetic exchange -- genetic information passes from a donor cell to a recipient cell, rather than two cells fusing their genomes symmetrically as in true (meiotic) sexual reproduction. Transformation, conjugation and transduction are all specific mechanisms that carry out this same underlying unilateral, parasexual pattern of transfer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transcription is an entirely separate, intracellular process (making RNA from a DNA template); it does not describe transfer of genetic material between two different cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify "parasexuality" as the general term for bacteria's unilateral, donor-to-recipient pattern of genetic exchange.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Conjugative plasmid characteristics
questions.question: All of the following are characters of conjugative plasmids EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a genuine character, so not the EXCEPT answer). Conjugative plasmids characteristically transfer at a high frequency between bacterial cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect (genuine character). Conjugative plasmids characteristically show a wide range of hosts they can be transferred into, often crossing species and genus boundaries.
explanations.C: Incorrect (genuine character). Conjugative plasmids characteristically carry multiple genetic determinants (such as several resistance or virulence genes together) on the same plasmid.
explanations.D: Correct. All three listed properties -- high transfer frequency, wide host range, and multiple genetic determinants -- are genuine, well-recognised characters of conjugative plasmids, so none of them is a false statement to be excepted. Since the question asks which is NOT a genuine character and every option offered is in fact true, "none of the above" is the only answer consistent with all three being correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that high transfer frequency, wide host range, and multiple genetic determinants are all genuine characters of conjugative plasmids, with no exception among them.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Gene therapy: replacing a mutated gene
questions.question: Replacing the mutated form of a gene in the original host cell with a healthy form of that gene?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Replacement therapy" is a generic clinical term (used, for example, for hormone or enzyme replacement) that does not specifically name the technique of substituting a healthy gene copy for a mutated one within a cell.
explanations.B: Correct. Gene therapy is, by definition, the technique of replacing the mutated (disease-causing) form of a gene in the patient's own host cell with a healthy, functional copy of that gene, with the aim of correcting the underlying genetic disorder rather than only managing its symptoms. This gene-level substitution -- inserting a working copy where a faulty one exists -- is exactly what distinguishes gene therapy from simply reading a sequence (DNA sequencing) or mapping gene locations (genetic mapping).
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA sequencing is the process of reading out a DNA molecule's nucleotide order; it identifies a mutation but does not itself replace or correct it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Genetic mapping is the process of locating genes or markers along a chromosome; it does not involve replacing a mutated gene with a healthy copy.

questions.learning_objective: Define gene therapy as replacing a mutated gene in the host cell with a healthy copy, distinguishing it from replacement therapy generically, DNA sequencing, and genetic mapping.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: DNA probe: a labeled sequence derived from the sought organism
questions.question: Short sequence of labeled single stranded DNA or RNA originally derived from the organism being sought?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A primer is a short segment that provides a starting point for DNA polymerase to extend a new strand; it initiates DNA synthesis rather than being used to detect a target sequence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A promoter is a regulatory DNA sequence upstream of a gene where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription; it is not a labeled molecule derived from a sought organism and used as a detection reagent.
explanations.C: Correct. A DNA (or RNA) probe is, by definition, a short, labeled, single-stranded sequence originally derived from the organism being sought, used to detect a complementary sequence in a test sample through hybridization. This detection role -- finding a matching sequence, not initiating synthesis (a primer's job) or regulating transcription (a promoter's job) -- is exactly what the term "probe" describes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. As printed, option D repeats option B's text ("Promotor") rather than offering a distinct fourth choice -- a source-side print defect that does not affect this question's answerability, since option C remains the unambiguously correct, uniquely worded choice.

questions.learning_objective: Define a DNA/RNA probe as a short labeled single-stranded sequence derived from the sought organism, distinguishing it from a primer or promoter.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.author_notes: Source prints option D identical to option B ("Promotor" twice) -- preserved as printed rather than invented over, since it does not create any ambiguity about the correct answer (C). A near-duplicate of this fact recurs at Ch4 Q40, held rather than authored twice.

questions.title: Order of PCR steps
questions.question: Steps of PCR in order are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This places both annealing and extension before denaturation, but primers cannot anneal to a template that has not yet been denatured into single strands.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This places extension before annealing and both before denaturation; extension requires an already-annealed primer, and annealing requires an already-denatured template, so this order violates both dependencies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This places extension before annealing; a primer must anneal to its complementary template sequence before DNA polymerase can extend it, so extension cannot come first.
explanations.D: Correct. Each PCR cycle proceeds through denaturation, then annealing, then extension, in that fixed order. DNA denaturation (heating to separate the double-stranded template into single strands) must come first, because primer annealing (cooling to let short primers bind their complementary sequences) needs single-stranded template to bind. Primer extension (a heat-stable DNA polymerase extending the primers) comes last, since it needs those primers already annealed before it can begin synthesizing new complementary strands.

questions.learning_objective: State the correct order of PCR's three steps -- denaturation, then annealing, then extension -- and why each depends on the step before it.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Applications of nucleic acid probes: the exception
questions.question: All of the following are applications of nucleic acid probes EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a genuine application, so not the EXCEPT answer). Nucleic acid probes are used to detect pathogen-specific sequences, a standard tool in diagnosing infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect (genuine application). Probes are used to detect cancer-associated gene sequences or rearrangements, a standard tool in cancer diagnosis.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the exception, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Amplifying DNA is the job of PCR (using primers and a heat-stable DNA polymerase to make many copies of a target sequence), not the job of a nucleic acid probe, whose role is detecting a complementary sequence by hybridization rather than copying it.
explanations.D: Incorrect (genuine application). Hybridization experiments are the core mechanism by which a probe finds and binds its complementary target sequence -- this is the probe's defining use, not an exception to it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify infection diagnosis, cancer diagnosis and hybridization as genuine applications of nucleic acid probes, and DNA amplification (a PCR/primer function) as the exception.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Gene cassette characteristics
questions.question: Gene cassettes are characterized by?

options.A: Exists freely or incorporated into an integron

explanations.A: Correct. A gene cassette is characterised by being able to exist freely (as a circular molecule) or become incorporated into a larger genetic platform called an integron. This freely-existing-or-integron-incorporated duality is the cassette's own defining property, distinct from the integrase enzyme and attI recombination site, both of which belong to the integron that captures the cassette, not to the cassette itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The integrase enzyme that captures and mobilises gene cassettes belongs to the integron, not to the cassette itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A gene cassette is typically a small element carrying one, or occasionally a small number of, genes -- "contains multiple genes" overstates what a single cassette characteristically carries.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The attI recombination site, which the integron's integrase uses to capture a cassette, belongs to the integron, not to the gene cassette itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that a gene cassette can exist freely or become incorporated into an integron, and that the integrase enzyme and attI site belong to the integron, not the cassette.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 4, p50

questions.title: Plasmid classification
questions.question: Plasmid is a?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plasma protein is a blood-serum molecule (such as albumin or a clotting factor); a plasmid is DNA, not a protein, and has no connection to blood plasma.
explanations.B: Correct. A plasmid is, at the broadest classification level, a genetic factor -- a small, circular, extrachromosomal DNA element that carries accessory genetic information and can replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome. This "genetic factor" classification is what separates a plasmid from a protein, a granule, or a membrane component, none of which are genetic (DNA-carrying) elements at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A serum factor is a blood-plasma component (unrelated terminology, similarly to "plasma protein"); a plasmid is a bacterial genetic element, not a component of blood serum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cytoplasmic (inclusion) granules are nutrient-storage deposits within the cell, not genetic material -- an entirely different kind of structure from a plasmid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The plasma membrane is the cell's lipid bilayer boundary; a plasmid is a free-floating cytoplasmic DNA molecule, not a component of the membrane.

questions.learning_objective: Classify a plasmid as a genetic factor, distinguishing it from a plasma protein, serum factor, cytoplasmic granule, or membrane component.

questions.title: Mutation: a heritable change in the genome
questions.question: Heritable changes in genome are called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Conjugation is a mechanism of transferring DNA between two bacterial cells; it is not itself an alteration of the genome's sequence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transduction is a bacteriophage-mediated mechanism of DNA transfer between cells; it is not itself a change in the genome's sequence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transformation is uptake of free DNA by a competent recipient cell; it is a transfer mechanism, not itself a heritable sequence change.
explanations.D: Correct. A heritable change in the genome is, by definition, a mutation -- a permanent alteration of the DNA sequence that is copied into every subsequent generation of the cell. This heritability, arising from the change being replicated along with the rest of the genome at every division, is exactly what distinguishes mutation from the various gene-transfer mechanisms (conjugation, transduction, transformation), none of which by themselves alter a sequence.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Replication, when accurate, copies the existing DNA sequence faithfully; it is the process a mutation can be perpetuated through, not the name for the heritable change itself.

questions.learning_objective: Define mutation as a heritable change in the genome, distinguishing it from conjugation, transduction, transformation and replication.

questions.title: Bacterium most used in genetic engineering
questions.question: The Bacterium that is most commonly used in genetic engineering is?

explanations.A: Correct. Escherichia coli is the bacterium most commonly used as a host organism in genetic engineering and recombinant DNA technology, owing to its well-characterised genetics, rapid growth, and the wide availability of plasmid vectors and molecular tools that have been developed specifically for it over decades of research. This combination of practical advantages is why E. coli, rather than the other Gram-negative enteric bacteria listed, became the standard laboratory workhorse species for this purpose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Klebsiella is a clinically important Gram-negative pathogen, but it is not the standard laboratory host species used for genetic engineering the way E. coli is.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Proteus is a clinically important Gram-negative pathogen, but it is not the standard laboratory host species used for genetic engineering the way E. coli is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Serratia is a Gram-negative bacterium of some clinical and industrial interest, but it is not the standard laboratory host species used for genetic engineering the way E. coli is.

questions.learning_objective: State that Escherichia coli, not Klebsiella, Proteus or Serratia, is the bacterium most commonly used as a genetic engineering host organism.
